domain_label: Study System — Visual-Encoding Cartographer: Color System & Meaning Encoding
purpose: A method for turning the study app's knowledge-graph semantics — taxonomy role, high-yield importance, and per-node mastery state — into color that is perceptually honest, decodable, and colorblind-safe on a dark theme: choosing a perceptual color space (CIELAB/HCL, OKLCH) so that equal color steps read as equal meaning steps, assigning hue to nominal category and lightness/chroma to ordinal magnitude, brightness to high-yield weight, discrete state colors plus a corner indicator dot to mastery, and enforcing WCAG contrast and CVD-safe separation with redundant non-color channels — kept honest by tagging color-science claims ESTIMATE-to-source-verify (none are verified in EXTERNAL_RECON here), grounding the mastery-color and no-graph-library facts in APP_RECON, and never fabricating a WCAG number, palette name, or citation.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors and every palette/threshold choice is an ESTIMATE synthesized from general color-science knowledge

the app is a single-user, dark-themed React 18 / Vite app and no graph library is installed yet, so this KB specifies the color system a future graph view and analytics charts will consume rather than an existing renderer [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.5]

color-science references (CIELAB, HCL, OKLCH, WCAG contrast ratios, Okabe-Ito, ColorBrewer, viridis) are named from general domain knowledge and are NOT source-verified in EXTERNAL_RECON, so each is tagged [ESTIMATE — to source-verify] and no exact ratio, hex, or citation is invented

the existing app already colors mastery bars green >=60% / yellow >=40% / red below [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.9 MasteryBars], and this KB extends that convention to graph nodes rather than replacing it
graph layout, semantic-zoom geometry, edge bundling, and the analytics-chart catalog beyond color are neighboring KBs in the same specialist that this KB depends on but does not specify
exclusions: graph layout algorithms, force-directed placement, edge bundling and semantic-zoom geometry (neighboring viz KB) beyond how color behaves across zoom levels
the analytics-chart type catalog (calibration trends, mastery-over-time line/bar/heatmap selection) beyond the color ramps those charts consume
typography, iconography, spacing and the non-color visual language of the UI shell

the meaning of the underlying quantities themselves (BKT mastery, Elo difficulty, FSRS retrievability, high-yield weight) which are owned by the learner and content specialists — this KB only encodes them
implementation of a specific CSS/canvas/WebGL renderer or a specific color library, beyond requiring a computed-token indirection layer

competency_questions.question: What is the color-encoding problem for the knowledge-graph view, and what three meanings must color carry?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states the goal of mapping taxonomy role, high-yield importance, and mastery state onto color perceptually and colorblind-safely on a dark theme, and notes no graph library exists yet so this is a spec for a future renderer, citing APP_RECON §5.5

competency_questions.question: Why are sRGB/HSL/HSV the wrong spaces to encode magnitude, and what does perceptual non-uniformity mean?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: explains that equal numeric steps in sRGB/HSL are unequal perceptual steps (a yellow at a given HSL lightness looks far brighter than a blue), so an HSL ramp mis-encodes magnitude, motivating a perceptually uniform space, tagged ESTIMATE-to-source-verify

competency_questions.question: What are CIELAB and its HCL/LCh polar form, and why is the polar form the design-friendly control surface?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: defines CIELAB L*/a*/b* with Delta-E as an approximately perceptual distance and HCL as its cylindrical (hue angle, chroma, lightness) reparameterization, noting hue-for-category and lightness-for-magnitude fall out of separating the polar axes, tagged ESTIMATE-to-source-verify

competency_questions.question: What does OKLab/OKLCH improve over CIELAB-HCL and when should it be preferred?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states OKLab/OKLCH is a newer perceptual space with better hue linearity (notably through blue) and predictable lightness, making uniform ramps and hue-holding easier, and is CSS-native, while noting the choice between it and CIELAB-HCL is an ESTIMATE not benchmarked here

competency_questions.question: Which color channel encodes which kind of data variable, per the graphical-perception tradition?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states hue is a nominal/categorical channel and lightness (and secondarily chroma) is an ordinal/magnitude channel, per the Bertin / Cleveland-McGill-tradition ranking, and that mismatching them (hue for magnitude) is a decoding error, tagged ESTIMATE-to-source-verify

competency_questions.question: How are distinct hues assigned to taxonomy roles, how many are safely distinguishable, and how do related shades mark related concepts along an edge?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: assigns distinct categorical hues to taxonomy roles (e.g. pathology vs mechanism vs treatment), caps simultaneously distinguishable categorical hues at roughly 7-8, and uses analogous/near hues (related shades) for related concepts so an edge between kin reads as a small hue step, tagged ESTIMATE

competency_questions.question: How does brightness encode high-yield importance, and why brightness rather than hue?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: maps higher high-yield weight to higher luminance/brightness (an ordinal magnitude channel) so important nodes are visually salient, keeps it orthogonal to the taxonomy hue, and notes the dark-theme luminance floor limits the usable range, tagged ESTIMATE

competency_questions.question: How is per-node mastery state colored (green=known, gray=unasked) and why is the intensity/red-dot indicator a separate corner mark?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: colors mastery as discrete states (green known, gray unasked, extending the app's existing green>=60/yellow>=40/red bars) and moves the weakness-intensity indicator to a corner dot so it does not fight the node-fill's taxonomy hue and yield brightness, citing APP_RECON §5.9

competency_questions.question: What makes the palette colorblind-safe and why must meaning be redundantly encoded off the color channel?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: names the common CVD types (deuteranopia/protanopia red-green, tritanopia blue-yellow), forbids red-vs-green as the sole distinction, points to CVD-safe palettes (Okabe-Ito, viridis/cividis, ColorBrewer safe sets), and requires a second non-color channel (shape, position, dot, label) so meaning survives CVD and grayscale, tagged ESTIMATE

competency_questions.question: What contrast and gamut constraints does a dark theme impose, and how are they checked?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states WCAG contrast targets (text ~4.5:1, large text/non-text UI ~3:1) as the accessibility floor, notes achievable chroma varies with hue and lightness and clips at the display gamut so not every HCL triple is realizable, and requires validating computed colors against both, all tagged ESTIMATE-to-source-verify

competency_questions.question: How are sequential/diverging/categorical palettes built, and how does simultaneous contrast distort small colored nodes?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: distinguishes categorical (vary hue), sequential (monotone lightness ramp) and diverging (two ramps about a neutral midpoint) palettes built in a perceptual space, and warns that a small node's color shifts perceptually against its background and neighbors (simultaneous contrast), so small marks need higher chroma and a validated background, tagged ESTIMATE

competency_questions.question: How does color stay honest across semantic zoom, and what computed-token system and final verdict tie the whole scheme together?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: keeps a cluster's aggregate hue and honestly-aggregated brightness when zoomed out, routes every color through named semantic tokens computed from HCL/OKLCH so meaning has one source of truth, and states the go verdict (perceptual-space tokens; hue=taxonomy, brightness=yield, discrete mastery states + corner dot; CVD-safe + WCAG + redundant encoding) and the no-gos (no raw sRGB/HSL ramps, no hue-for-magnitude, no red-green-only, no hardcoded hex)

glossary.definition: A color space engineered so that geometric distance approximates perceived color difference — CIELAB (CIE 1976 L*a*b*) and its cylindrical HCL/LCh form, and the newer OKLab/OKLCH — as opposed to device spaces (sRGB) or naive cylinders (HSL/HSV) where equal numeric steps are perceptually unequal [ESTIMATE — to source-verify].

The three polar axes of a perceptual space: hue = the angular 'which color' (nominal), chroma = colorfulness/saturation distance from gray, lightness = perceived brightness (ordinal). Separating them lets one channel carry category and another carry magnitude without cross-talk [ESTIMATE — to source-verify].

The distance metric in CIELAB approximating how different two colors look; a Delta-E near the just-noticeable-difference threshold means two colors are barely distinguishable, which bounds how many categorical colors can coexist [ESTIMATE — to source-verify].

The graphical-perception assignment (Bertin's visual variables; the Cleveland-McGill perception tradition) that hue is a nominal channel best for unordered categories while lightness is an ordinal channel best for ordered magnitude; using hue for magnitude produces a rainbow ramp that cannot be read in order [ESTIMATE — to source-verify].

Mapping a concept's high-yield importance weight to node brightness/luminance so the exam-critical nodes are the visually salient ones, kept orthogonal to the taxonomy hue and the mastery state so the three meanings do not overwrite each other [ESTIMATE].

Discrete per-node knowledge-state coloring — green = known/mastered, gray = unasked/untested — extending the app's existing MasteryBars scheme (green >=60% / yellow >=40% / red below), with a corner indicator dot carrying weakness intensity so state does not fight the node-fill hue [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.9 for the existing bar thresholds; ESTIMATE for the graph-node extension].

A small mark in a node's corner that carries a fourth signal (mastery/weakness intensity) on a separate visual token from the node fill, so the fill can keep encoding taxonomy hue and yield brightness while the dot honestly shows knowledge state — a form of redundant/second-channel encoding [ESTIMATE].

A palette whose categories stay distinguishable under color-vision deficiency — deuteranopia/protanopia (red-green, ~8% of males) and the rarer tritanopia (blue-yellow) — by avoiding red-vs-green as a sole distinction and drawing from tested sets (Okabe-Ito, viridis/cividis, ColorBrewer safe palettes) [ESTIMATE — to source-verify].

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines luminance-contrast requirement — roughly 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text and non-text UI components — used here as the accessibility floor that every computed node/label/background color pair must pass, especially on the dark theme [ESTIMATE — to source-verify].

A named, meaning-carrying color variable (e.g. token 'taxonomy.pathology' or 'mastery.known') computed from HCL/OKLCH parameters, so that UI code references the meaning, not a raw hex, and the whole system can be re-tuned, gamut-clamped and contrast-checked in one place [ESTIMATE].

nodes.definition: Frame the color-encoding problem for the knowledge-graph view: color must carry THREE distinct meanings at once on each node — (1) taxonomy role (which kind of concept: pathology vs mechanism vs treatment), (2) high-yield importance (how exam-critical), and (3) mastery state (known / unasked / weak) — plus edges relate kin concepts. This is a mapping problem from data semantics to perceptual channels, and it must be perceptually honest (equal color steps = equal meaning steps), colorblind-safe, and legible on the app's dark theme. No graph library is installed and no page renders any graph yet, so this KB specifies the color system a FUTURE renderer and the analytics charts will consume, not an existing one [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.5 — no graph library installed, no page renders a graph]. Three simultaneous meanings on one small mark is the core tension the rest of the KB resolves by spreading them across orthogonal channels (hue, brightness, a separate state token).

included: the three color-borne meanings (taxonomy role, high-yield, mastery state) plus edge kinship
the honest/colorblind-safe/dark-theme constraints
the spec-for-a-future-renderer framing
excluded: graph layout and semantic-zoom geometry (neighboring KB)
the specific color spaces and channel assignments (later nodes)

pros.claim: Naming the three simultaneous meanings up front forces them onto orthogonal channels instead of one overloaded color
pros.example: deciding early that hue carries taxonomy, brightness carries yield, and a corner dot carries mastery rather than cramming all three into one fill color

cons.claim: The three-meanings framing is a design judgment about what matters, which a real user study could revise
cons.example: assuming taxonomy role deserves the hue channel before any evidence that users navigate by role rather than by mastery

failure_modes: overloading a single color to mean role, yield and mastery at once so none is decodable
designing the color system as if a renderer already exists and constraints are fixed
acceptance_tests: the frame lists the three color-borne meanings plus edge kinship, states the honest/colorblind-safe/dark-theme constraints, and notes the no-graph-library spec-for-future framing with the APP_RECON citation
revisit_triggers: a graph library is chosen and its color API constrains the design
user testing shows a different meaning deserves the salient channel
a fourth per-node meaning must be encoded

base.update_signal: a chosen graph library or a user-study finding revises which meanings color must carry

nodes.definition: Establish why device and naive spaces are the wrong place to encode meaning: sRGB, HSL and HSV are perceptually NON-UNIFORM — equal numeric steps do not look like equal color steps. In HSL, a fully saturated yellow at lightness 50% is far brighter and more salient than a fully saturated blue at the same nominal lightness, so an HSL 'lightness ramp' mis-encodes magnitude and an HSL hue wheel spends most of its arc in greens [ESTIMATE — to source-verify; classic color-science result]. Encoding an ordered quantity (yield, mastery) in such a space produces a ramp a viewer cannot read monotonically. This is the whole reason to move to a perceptual space (CIELAB/HCL, OKLCH) where a fixed lightness delta looks like a fixed brightness change regardless of hue. Naive spaces are fine for picking a single color, wrong for encoding a scale.

included: the perceptual non-uniformity of sRGB/HSL/HSV
why an HSL ramp mis-encodes magnitude
the motivation for a perceptual space
excluded: the CIELAB/OKLCH definitions themselves (next nodes)
the channel-to-meaning assignment

pros.claim: Ruling out HSL/sRGB for scales prevents the most common encoding bug — an unreadable rainbow or uneven lightness ramp
pros.example: rejecting an HSL yield ramp because its yellow midpoint spikes in brightness and breaks the perceived order

cons.claim: Perceptual spaces cost a conversion step and are less familiar than the hex/HSL most developers reach for
cons.example: a developer hardcoding an HSL value because the toolchain lacks an HCL/OKLCH helper

failure_modes: building a sequential or brightness ramp directly in HSL and getting non-monotone perceived lightness
assuming HSL 'lightness' equals perceived brightness
acceptance_tests: the node explains that equal sRGB/HSL steps are perceptually unequal, gives the yellow-vs-blue brightness example, and concludes a perceptual space is required for any scale, tagged ESTIMATE-to-source-verify

nodes.definition: Define CIELAB (CIE 1976 L*a*b*) as the reference perceptual space: L* is perceived lightness (0 black to 100 white), a* is the green-red axis, b* is the blue-yellow axis, and Euclidean distance between two colors, Delta-E, approximates their perceived difference [ESTIMATE — to source-verify; standard colorimetry]. A Delta-E near the just-noticeable-difference threshold means two colors are barely distinguishable, which directly bounds how many categorical colors can coexist and how fine a sequential ramp can be. CIELAB is device-independent and the historical basis for perceptual palette design, but its Cartesian a*/b* axes are awkward for a designer who thinks in 'hue' and 'saturation' — which is why the polar HCL reparameterization (next node) is the working control surface. CIELAB is the yardstick; HCL is the steering wheel.

included: the L*/a*/b* axes and their meaning
Delta-E as an approximately perceptual distance and its JND interpretation
CIELAB as the basis for the polar HCL form
excluded: the HCL polar controls themselves (next node)
the OKLCH refinement

pros.claim: A perceptual distance metric lets category count and ramp fineness be reasoned about quantitatively rather than by eye
pros.example: spacing categorical hues so each pair exceeds a comfortable Delta-E and stays distinguishable

cons.claim: CIELAB's uniformity is only approximate and its Cartesian axes are unintuitive for direct design
cons.example: a designer struggling to raise 'saturation' when it means moving in both a* and b* at once

failure_modes: treating Delta-E as an exact perceptual truth rather than an approximation
designing directly in a*/b* and losing the hue/chroma intuition
acceptance_tests: the node defines L*/a*/b*, gives Delta-E as an approximately perceptual distance with the JND-bounds-category-count consequence, and motivates the polar HCL form, tagged ESTIMATE-to-source-verify
revisit_triggers: a newer difference metric (CIEDE2000 refinement) is adopted
OKLCH replaces CIELAB as the working space
measured Delta-E thresholds are calibrated for the display

base.update_signal: a refined difference metric or a space swap changes the yardstick

nodes.definition: Give HCL/LCh as the polar reparameterization of CIELAB and the working control surface for the whole system: Hue (angle around the a*b* plane, the nominal 'which color'), Chroma (radial distance from the neutral axis, colorfulness), Lightness (the L* axis, perceived brightness) [ESTIMATE — to source-verify]. The design payoff is orthogonality: you can hold hue fixed and vary lightness to build a sequential ramp, or hold lightness and chroma fixed and vary hue to build a categorical set, and each control changes one perceived attribute. This separation is exactly what the channel-to-meaning map needs — hue for category, lightness/chroma for magnitude — and it is why palette construction, gamut checks and contrast checks all happen in HCL/OKLCH rather than in hex. HCL is the coordinate system every downstream color decision is expressed in.

included: the H/C/L polar axes as a reparameterization of CIELAB
the orthogonality payoff for holding one attribute while varying another
HCL as the coordinate system for palettes, gamut and contrast work
excluded: the specific channel-to-meaning assignment (its own node)
OKLCH's refinements

pros.claim: Orthogonal H/C/L controls let each meaning be tied to exactly one perceived attribute, keeping the channels independent
pros.example: building a five-step yield ramp by moving only L while H and C stay pinned to the taxonomy color

cons.claim: Not every (H,C,L) triple is realizable on a real display, so the intuitive control can propose out-of-gamut colors
cons.example: asking for a high-chroma blue at high lightness that the sRGB gamut cannot produce and must be clamped

failure_modes: assuming any hue supports the same chroma at any lightness (it does not)
editing hue and accidentally shifting perceived lightness because of a non-perceptual tool
acceptance_tests: the node defines H/C/L as CIELAB in polar form, shows the hold-one-vary-another orthogonality, and names HCL as the coordinate system for palette/gamut/contrast work
revisit_triggers: OKLCH is adopted as the primary polar space

a channel assignment changes which axis carries which meaning

base.update_signal: an OKLCH switch or persistent gamut distortion changes the control surface

nodes.definition: Record OKLab and its polar form OKLCH as the modern refinement of the CIELAB-HCL approach: a perceptual space with better HUE LINEARITY — holding OKLCH hue constant while changing lightness keeps the perceived hue steadier than CIELAB, which drifts (notably the blue-to-purple Bezold-Brucke-style shift), and lightness is more predictable — and it is natively supported in CSS Color 4 (oklch()) [ESTIMATE — to source-verify]. The practical consequence is that sequential ramps and hold-the-hue categorical variations are easier to build correctly in OKLCH, and colors can be authored directly in stylesheets. This KB treats OKLCH and CIELAB-HCL as interchangeable at the level of principle (hue=category, lightness=magnitude) and flags the choice between them as an implementation ESTIMATE, not benchmarked here; whichever is used, all reasoning stays in a perceptual polar space, never raw sRGB.

included: OKLab/OKLCH as a hue-linear perceptual space with CSS-native support
why it eases uniform ramps and hue-holding
treating it and CIELAB-HCL as interchangeable in principle
excluded: a benchmarked comparison of the two spaces (not done here)
the channel-to-meaning assignment

pros.claim: Better hue linearity and CSS-native syntax make correct ramps easier and let colors live in the stylesheet as computed values
pros.example: authoring a yield ramp as oklch() steps that hold hue and only raise lightness

cons.claim: The CIELAB-vs-OKLCH choice is unbenchmarked here and older browsers/tools may lack OKLCH support, forcing a fallback
cons.example: shipping an sRGB fallback for a browser that does not parse oklch()

failure_modes: claiming OKLCH is strictly better without a benchmark
relying on oklch() where the runtime cannot parse it and getting no fallback
acceptance_tests: the node states OKLCH's hue-linearity and CSS-native advantages, treats it as interchangeable-in-principle with CIELAB-HCL, and flags the choice as an unbenchmarked ESTIMATE

nodes.definition: Account for the display gamut and the dark-theme background as hard limits on which HCL/OKLCH colors are realizable. The set of achievable chroma is not a cylinder: maximum chroma varies strongly with both hue and lightness (yellows reach high chroma only at high lightness; blues sit at lower lightness), so requesting a high-chroma color at the wrong lightness pushes outside the sRGB gamut and must be CLAMPED — reducing chroma or nudging lightness — which can silently collapse two intended-distinct colors together [ESTIMATE — to source-verify]. On the app's dark theme, node colors sit on a near-black background, which raises the usable lightness floor (very dark nodes vanish) and interacts with contrast requirements. Every computed token must therefore be gamut-mapped and re-checked after clamping, not assumed to render as authored.

included: hue- and lightness-dependent maximum chroma and gamut clamping
the dark-theme lightness floor for node visibility
the requirement to re-check colors after clamping
excluded: the WCAG contrast math itself (its own node)
wide-gamut/P3 displays beyond noting sRGB as the assumed target

pros.claim: Gamut-checking each token stops the palette from silently collapsing distinct colors when the display cannot render them
pros.example: detecting that a clamped high-chroma yellow and its neighbor now differ by less than a JND and re-spacing them

cons.claim: Gamut limits constrain the design so intended hue/chroma/lightness combinations may be unavailable, forcing compromise

failure_modes: authoring colors that clamp out of gamut and render as near-duplicates

nodes.definition: State the core assignment of perceptual channels to data-variable types, the spine of the whole encoding: HUE is a NOMINAL/categorical channel — best for unordered categories, poor for order — and LIGHTNESS (with chroma as a secondary, weaker magnitude cue) is an ORDINAL/quantitative channel — read monotonically as more-or-less. This follows the graphical-perception tradition (Bertin's visual variables; the Cleveland-McGill lineage of perception experiments ranking encodings by decoding accuracy) [ESTIMATE — to source-verify]. The consequence for this app: taxonomy role (unordered) takes hue; high-yield importance and mastery magnitude (ordered) take lightness/brightness. The classic error this forbids is the rainbow ramp — encoding an ordered quantity in hue — which viewers cannot decode in order because hue has no perceptual ranking. Every later node is an application of this one rule.

included: hue as the nominal/categorical channel
lightness (and secondary chroma) as the ordinal/magnitude channel
the forbidden rainbow-ramp error
excluded: the specific taxonomy hue assignment (its own node)
the yield brightness ramp (its own node)

pros.claim: A single channel-to-variable rule makes every later color decision a consistent application rather than an ad-hoc choice
pros.example: immediately knowing yield must be a lightness ramp and taxonomy must be a hue set, not the reverse

cons.claim: The rule caps how much can be encoded — only a few channels exist, so a fourth ordered variable has nowhere clean to go
cons.example: needing to show yield, mastery magnitude and recency all as ordered and running out of orthogonal magnitude channels

failure_modes: encoding an ordered quantity in hue and producing an unreadable rainbow
encoding a category in lightness so unrelated groups look ranked
acceptance_tests: the node assigns hue to nominal/category and lightness (with secondary chroma) to ordinal/magnitude per the Bertin/Cleveland-McGill tradition and forbids hue-for-magnitude, tagged ESTIMATE-to-source-verify
revisit_triggers: a fourth data variable needs a channel

base.update_signal: a new variable or a revised perception ranking changes the assignment

nodes.definition: Apply hue as the categorical channel to taxonomy ROLE: assign distinct, well-separated hues to the unordered concept roles the domain distinguishes (for example pathology vs mechanism vs treatment vs anatomy), so a node's fill hue answers 'what kind of concept is this' at a glance. Perceptual and cognitive limits cap the number of hues a viewer can reliably tell apart and remember simultaneously at roughly 7-8 categorical colors [ESTIMATE — to source-verify; classic categorical-palette guidance]; beyond that, either group finer categories under a parent hue or use a second channel. Hues are spaced for near-equal Delta-E and equal lightness/chroma so no role looks more important merely from its color, keeping the yield-brightness channel free to carry importance. Categorical hue must never imply order — roles are peers.

included: assigning distinct hues to unordered taxonomy roles
the ~7-8 distinguishable-hue cap and how to exceed it (nesting, second channel)
equalizing lightness/chroma so no role looks pre-ranked
excluded: related-shade edges between kin concepts (its own node)
the CVD-safety constraint on the hue set (its own node)

pros.claim: Distinct role hues let a viewer classify every node by kind pre-attentively without reading labels
pros.example: seeing all treatment nodes share one hue and all pathology nodes another across a dense subgraph

cons.claim: The ~7-8 hue ceiling means a taxonomy with many roles overflows the channel and needs nesting or a second cue
cons.example: a ten-role taxonomy where the last roles are no longer reliably distinguishable by hue alone

failure_modes: assigning more categorical hues than are distinguishable and having roles blur together
letting one role's hue read as more important because of unequal lightness/chroma
acceptance_tests: the node assigns distinct hues to unordered roles, caps distinguishable categorical hues at roughly 7-8 with a nesting/second-channel escape, and equalizes lightness/chroma so no role looks pre-ranked, tagged ESTIMATE
revisit_triggers: the taxonomy gains more roles than distinguishable hues

base.update_signal: a taxonomy growth or a role-confusion finding changes the hue assignment

nodes.definition: Apply lightness/brightness as the magnitude channel to HIGH-YIELD importance: map a higher high-yield weight to a higher-luminance node so the exam-critical concepts are literally the brightest, most salient marks, while low-yield nodes recede darker. Brightness is a strong pre-attentive magnitude cue and reads monotonically, which matches how importance should be scanned [ESTIMATE — to source-verify]. Crucially this stays ORTHOGONAL to the taxonomy hue — importance rides lightness, role rides hue — so a bright pathology node and a bright treatment node are both important yet still distinct in kind. The dark theme caps the range: the darkest low-yield node must stay above the background lightness floor (from the gamut node) or it disappears, so the yield ramp spans a usable mid-to-high lightness band rather than the full 0-100.

included: mapping high-yield weight to node luminance/brightness
keeping brightness orthogonal to taxonomy hue
the dark-theme usable-lightness band for the ramp
excluded: the mastery-state coloring (its own node)
the WCAG contrast floor mechanics (its own node)

pros.claim: Brightness makes importance pre-attentive so the eye lands on high-yield nodes first without any legend
pros.example: a cluster where the two brightest nodes are the must-know concepts and the dim ones are peripheral

cons.claim: Brightness now carries yield, so it cannot also be freely used for mastery magnitude without collision, and the dark-theme range is narrow
cons.example: wanting to dim un-mastered nodes while brightness already means low-yield, conflating the two

failure_modes: reusing brightness for a second magnitude (mastery) and colliding with yield
letting low-yield nodes fall below the dark-theme visibility floor
acceptance_tests: the node maps yield to brightness monotonically, keeps it orthogonal to hue, and constrains the ramp to a dark-theme-safe lightness band above the visibility floor, tagged ESTIMATE
revisit_triggers: a second magnitude variable competes for the brightness channel
the dark-theme background lightness changes the usable band
yield weights are recomputed by the content specialist

base.update_signal: a competing magnitude channel or a theme change reworks the yield ramp

nodes.definition: Encode concept KINSHIP with related shades so an edge between related concepts reads as a small hue step, not a jump: concepts sharing a parent role or a strong 'related' edge get analogous (near-neighbor) hues within their role's hue neighborhood, so a family of related concepts forms a visually coherent band and an edge between kin connects two similar colors [ESTIMATE — to source-verify; analogous-color design principle]. This complements the categorical hue assignment: across roles hue jumps (distinct categories), within a role's related cluster hue varies gently (degrees of kinship). It gives the graph a readable large-scale structure — role islands of a shared hue family — without adding a channel. The limit is that gentle within-role hue steps must stay above a JND or kin become indistinguishable, so kinship shading is coarse, not a continuous similarity metric.

included: analogous/near hues for kin concepts within a role
edges between kin reading as small hue steps
role islands as large-scale readable structure
excluded: the cross-role distinct-hue assignment (prior node)
edge-line color/bundling geometry (neighboring layout KB)

pros.claim: Related shades give the graph legible neighborhoods so kinship is visible without reading edges one by one
pros.example: a band of near-teal nodes reading instantly as one related concept family within the mechanism role

nodes.definition: Color per-node knowledge state as DISCRETE states, not a continuous fill, because mastery is read as a small set of decisions: green = known/mastered, gray = unasked/untested (never presented), with the weak/at-risk state carried by an intensity indicator (next node). This extends the app's EXISTING convention — MasteryBars already colors mastery green >=60% / yellow >=40% / red below [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.9 MasteryBars] — into the graph so the two views agree. Gray for unasked is deliberate: an untested concept is unknown-state, not low-mastery, and must not read as red 'weak'. Discrete states are chosen over a smooth green-to-red fill because a smooth mastery fill would (a) fight the yield-brightness and taxonomy-hue channels for the same node fill and (b) rely on a red-green axis that fails under CVD — resolved by the separate corner dot.

nodes.definition: Carry the mastery/weakness INTENSITY on a corner indicator dot — a small mark on a separate visual token from the node fill — so the fill can keep encoding taxonomy hue and yield brightness while the dot honestly shows knowledge state and its urgency. A red-toned dot whose intensity/size scales with weakness severity (how far below mastery, how overdue) puts the 'attend to this' signal exactly where the eye can scan for it, without recoloring the whole node and destroying its role/yield encoding [ESTIMATE — design synthesis]. Placing state on a second token is the key move that resolves the three-meanings-on-one-mark tension from the frame: fill = role+yield, corner dot = state+intensity. The dot's position and shape also make it a redundant, non-hue channel that survives colorblindness (next nodes).

the dot as a scannable urgency cue

nodes.definition: Constrain the whole palette to be colorblind-safe (CVD-safe). The common deficiencies are deuteranopia and protanopia (red-green confusion, together affecting roughly 8% of males) and the rarer tritanopia (blue-yellow) [ESTIMATE — to source-verify]. The hard rules: never let red-vs-green be the SOLE distinction between two meanings (which directly threatens a naive green-known/red-weak mastery scheme, resolved by the corner dot's shape/position and by not relying on hue alone), keep categorical hues separable under simulated CVD, and prefer palettes designed and tested for this — Okabe-Ito for categorical, viridis/cividis for sequential, ColorBrewer's safe sets — rather than hand-picked hues [ESTIMATE — to source-verify; well-known palettes]. Every candidate palette is run through a CVD simulator and re-checked for Delta-E separation under each deficiency before shipping.

included: the CVD types and their prevalence
the never-red-green-alone rule and CVD-simulated separation checks
preferring tested palettes (Okabe-Ito, viridis/cividis, ColorBrewer)
excluded: the general redundant-encoding principle (next node)
the WCAG luminance-contrast requirement (its own node)

pros.claim: Designing CVD-safe from the start keeps the ~8% red-green-deficient users able to decode every meaning, not just the median viewer
pros.example: verifying that pathology and treatment hues stay separable under a deuteranopia simulation

cons.claim: CVD-safety shrinks the usable hue space, tightening an already ~7-8-category budget and sometimes forcing less-preferred colors
cons.example: dropping a natural red/green role pairing because it collapses under protanopia

failure_modes: shipping a red-green-only mastery or role distinction that vanishes under CVD
hand-picking hues that look distinct to the designer but collapse under simulation
acceptance_tests: the node names the CVD types, forbids red-green as a sole distinction, requires CVD-simulated Delta-E separation checks, and prefers tested palettes (Okabe-Ito/viridis/cividis/ColorBrewer), tagged ESTIMATE-to-source-verify

nodes.definition: Require every meaning color carries to be REDUNDANTLY encoded on at least one non-color channel — shape, position, size, a corner dot, a label, or a pattern — so the meaning survives colorblindness, grayscale printing, low-contrast displays and small marks where hue collapses [ESTIMATE — to source-verify; standard accessibility principle]. Concretely: mastery state is color AND the corner dot's shape/position; taxonomy role is hue AND (optionally) node shape or a glyph; yield is brightness AND size. Color is treated as an enhancement that speeds decoding, never as the only carrier of any critical distinction. This is the general principle behind the corner dot and the CVD rules: if removing all color still leaves the graph decodable, the encoding is robust; if it does not, a distinction is color-fragile and must gain a second channel.

included: the never-color-alone rule and its second-channel pairings
the grayscale-decodability test for robustness
color as enhancement not sole carrier
excluded: the specific CVD palette choices (prior node)
the WCAG contrast mechanics (next node)

pros.claim: A grayscale-decodable design is robust to CVD, printing, glare and tiny marks at once, not just to one failure mode
pros.example: the graph still readable when screenshotted in grayscale because shape and position carry the distinctions too

cons.claim: Second channels add complexity and can clutter dense views, and not every variable has a free redundant channel
cons.example: running out of distinct node shapes when both role and state already want a shape cue

failure_modes: leaving a critical distinction on color alone so it vanishes in grayscale/CVD
over-adding redundant cues until the view is cluttered
acceptance_tests: the node requires each color meaning to have a non-color redundant channel, gives the grayscale-decodability test, and states color is enhancement not sole carrier, tagged ESTIMATE
revisit_triggers: a distinction is found color-only in a grayscale test

a new meaning needs a redundant channel that is taken

base.update_signal: a grayscale-test failure or channel clutter changes the redundancy plan

nodes.definition: Enforce WCAG luminance contrast as the accessibility floor for every color pair the eye must resolve: roughly 4.5:1 for normal-size text and 3:1 for large text and non-text UI components (node outlines, the corner dot against the fill, labels against the background) [ESTIMATE — to source-verify]. On the dark theme this bites hardest for label text and for dim low-yield nodes against the near-black background, and it interacts with the yield-brightness ramp: the darkest usable node lightness is set by both the visibility floor (gamut node) AND the contrast requirement, whichever is higher. Every computed token pair — node vs background, label vs node, dot vs fill — is checked against its WCAG target after gamut clamping, and failing pairs are lightened or outlined rather than shipped. Contrast is a gate, not a preference.

included: the ~4.5:1 text and ~3:1 large/non-text contrast targets
the dark-theme label and dim-node contrast pressure
checking every token pair against WCAG after clamping
excluded: the gamut clamping itself (prior node)
the CVD-separation checks (its own node)

pros.claim: A hard contrast gate guarantees labels and marks stay readable for low-vision users and in glare, independent of taste
pros.example: auto-lightening a dim low-yield node's label until it clears 4.5:1 on the dark background

cons.claim: The contrast floor can override the intended yield-brightness ramp, compressing its dark end and reducing importance discrimination

failure_modes: shipping label or node colors below the WCAG threshold on the dark background

acceptance_tests: the node states the ~4.5:1 text and ~3:1 non-text targets as the floor, ties the dark-theme dark-end limit to the higher of visibility and contrast, and requires post-clamp checks of every pair, tagged ESTIMATE-to-source-verify

nodes.definition: Build the three palette families the app needs in a perceptual space, each matched to a data type: CATEGORICAL (vary hue at fixed lightness/chroma) for taxonomy roles and unordered chart series; SEQUENTIAL (a monotone lightness ramp at roughly constant hue) for ordered magnitudes like yield, mastery-over-time, or a heatmap of retrievability; DIVERGING (two sequential ramps meeting at a neutral light midpoint) for quantities with a meaningful center like calibration error (over- vs under-confident) or mastery change (gained vs lost) [ESTIMATE — to source-verify]. Each is constructed in HCL/OKLCH so steps are perceptually even, uses a CVD-safe base (viridis/cividis-style sequential, ColorBrewer diverging), and is the same machinery the analytics charts consume — the graph's node encoding and the charts share one palette system, so a color means the same thing in both.

building them in a perceptual space with a CVD-safe base
sharing the palette system between graph and charts
excluded: the specific chart-type catalog (neighboring analytics KB)
the simultaneous-contrast small-mark caveat (next node)

pros.example: using a diverging ramp for calibration error so over- and under-confidence read as opposite directions from a neutral center

nodes.definition: Account for simultaneous contrast and small-area color effects: the SAME color looks different depending on its surround — a node's fill shifts perceptually against the dark background and against its neighbors, and small marks lose apparent chroma and hue (the small-field tritanopia-like effect) so tiny nodes and thin corner dots read as more washed-out and less distinct than a large swatch of the identical color [ESTIMATE — to source-verify; classic perception effects]. Consequences: small nodes and dots need HIGHER chroma than a legend swatch to read as the intended color, categorical hues must be validated at the actual mark size on the actual dark background (not in a palette editor), and a color that separates well as a big swatch may collapse against neighbors when nodes pack densely. Validate colors in situ, at size, on the theme.

small-area chroma/hue loss requiring higher chroma for small marks
validating colors in situ at mark size on the dark theme
excluded: the palette-family construction (prior node)
the WCAG luminance math (its own node)

acceptance_tests: the node explains surround-dependent appearance and small-area chroma loss, requires higher chroma for small marks, and mandates in-situ validation at mark size on the dark theme, tagged ESTIMATE

nodes.definition: Keep color HONEST across semantic zoom, where zooming out replaces detail with abstraction (this KB's slice of the specialist's semantic-zoom scope): when many nodes collapse into a cluster glyph, the cluster's color must aggregate its members truthfully — take the dominant/shared taxonomy hue if the cluster is role-coherent (or a neutral/mixed hue if it spans roles, never a false single role), and set the cluster brightness from an honest aggregate of member yield (e.g. the max or a weighted mean, chosen and labeled, not a hue that implies a magnitude) [ESTIMATE — design synthesis]. Mastery corner dots aggregate into a cluster badge counting weak members rather than vanishing. The rule: an abstraction's color must not assert a precision or a category the detail does not support — zooming out may lose detail but must not lie.

included: truthful hue aggregation (dominant role or explicit mixed) for cluster glyphs
honest brightness aggregation of member yield with a stated rule
aggregating mastery dots into a cluster weak-count badge
excluded: the semantic-zoom geometry and clustering algorithm (neighboring layout KB)
the token system that stores the colors (next node)

pros.claim: Honest aggregation lets a zoomed-out cluster convey role and importance without fabricating a category or precision
pros.example: a mixed-role cluster shown neutral rather than borrowing one member's hue and implying it is all pathology

cons.claim: Truthful aggregation can look duller or vaguer than a confident single color, and the aggregate rule (max vs mean) is a judgment that shapes the message
cons.example: a neutral mixed-role cluster reading as less informative than a crisp single-hue one that would overclaim

nodes.definition: Route every color in the app through named SEMANTIC TOKENS computed from HCL/OKLCH parameters, so meaning has one source of truth and no component ever holds a raw hex. Tokens are named by meaning — 'taxonomy.pathology', 'yield.ramp.4', 'mastery.known', 'mastery.unasked', 'state.weak.dot' — and are generated by a single build step that: picks the HCL/OKLCH values, gamut-clamps them, runs the CVD-separation check, and runs the WCAG contrast check, emitting only colors that pass all three [ESTIMATE — design synthesis]. This indirection is what makes the whole system re-tunable (change one hue, everything updates), auditable (every token traces to a meaning and passes the gates), and consistent (graph and charts read the same tokens). A hardcoded hex anywhere is a defect because it escapes the gamut, CVD and contrast gates.

the single build step that gamut-clamps and CVD/WCAG-checks every token
the no-hardcoded-hex rule and graph/chart consistency

nodes.definition: Compose the recommended color system, the go/no-go this KB builds toward. GO: express all color in a perceptual polar space (CIELAB-HCL or OKLCH) and route it through computed semantic tokens; assign HUE to taxonomy role (distinct, equal-lightness, CVD-safe, ~7-8 max, analogous shades for kin), BRIGHTNESS to high-yield importance (monotone, dark-theme-safe band), and per-node MASTERY to discrete states (green=known, gray=unasked, extending the app's MasteryBars green>=60/yellow>=40/red [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.9]) with weakness intensity on a separate corner dot; redundantly encode every meaning on a non-color channel; gate every token through gamut, CVD-simulation and WCAG contrast; and aggregate color honestly across semantic zoom. NO-GO: no raw sRGB/HSL ramps, no hue-for-magnitude rainbows, no red-vs-green as a sole distinction, no hardcoded hex, and no cluster color that asserts a category or precision the detail lacks. A color earns a place only when it is perceptually correct, colorblind-safe, contrast-passing, and traceable to a meaning token.

included: the go stack (perceptual-space tokens; hue=taxonomy, brightness=yield, discrete mastery + corner dot; redundant encoding; gamut/CVD/WCAG gates; honest zoom aggregation)
the no-gos (no sRGB/HSL ramps, no hue-for-magnitude, no red-green-only, no hardcoded hex, no lying abstraction)
the perceptually-correct/CVD-safe/contrast-passing/token-traceable acceptance rule
excluded: graph layout and the analytics-chart catalog (neighboring KBs)

edge_cases.description: A high-chroma color clamps out of gamut and collapses onto its neighbor
edge_cases.trigger: an HCL/OKLCH triple is requested beyond the display gamut and silently clamped
edge_cases.mitigation: gamut-map every token and re-check Delta-E separation after clamping, re-spacing collapsed pairs

edge_cases.description: Label text on a dim low-yield node falls below the WCAG contrast floor
edge_cases.trigger: the yield ramp darkens a node until its label contrast drops under ~4.5:1
edge_cases.mitigation: clamp the dim end to the contrast floor or add an outline/plate behind the label

edge_cases.description: A zoomed-out mixed-role cluster is given one member's hue and implies a false category
edge_cases.trigger: cluster color aggregation takes an arbitrary member hue instead of testing role coherence
edge_cases.mitigation: use the dominant hue only when the cluster is role-coherent, otherwise a neutral/mixed color

edge_cases.description: The corner mastery dot becomes sub-pixel and invisible when zoomed out
edge_cases.trigger: the dot is rendered at a fixed tiny size regardless of zoom level
edge_cases.mitigation: aggregate dots into a cluster weak-count badge at low zoom rather than shrinking them to noise

edge_cases.description: A component ships a hardcoded hex that bypasses the gamut/CVD/contrast gates
edge_cases.trigger: a developer sets a raw color value instead of referencing a token
edge_cases.mitigation: lint against raw hex in components and require every color to resolve to a gated semantic token

edge_cases.description: A color-science threshold is stated as fact without source verification
edge_cases.trigger: a WCAG ratio, JND, or palette claim is asserted as verified when it is only general knowledge here
edge_cases.mitigation: tag every unverified color-science claim ESTIMATE-to-source-verify and confirm exact numbers in the L1 research pass before hardcoding

workflow.action: Frame the three color-borne meanings and constraints
workflow.description: State that color must carry taxonomy role, high-yield importance and mastery state honestly, colorblind-safely, on the dark theme, for a not-yet-built renderer
workflow.gate: the three meanings, the honest/CVD-safe/dark-theme constraints, and the no-graph-library framing (APP_RECON §5.5) are stated

workflow.description: Reject sRGB/HSL for scales and adopt CIELAB-HCL (or OKLCH) as the polar control surface with orthogonal H/C/L axes
workflow.gate: perceptual non-uniformity is shown, HCL/OKLCH is adopted with orthogonal axes, and the choice is tagged ESTIMATE

workflow.description: Fix hue = nominal category, lightness/chroma = ordinal magnitude, forbidding hue-for-magnitude rainbows
workflow.gate: hue is assigned to category and lightness to magnitude per the perception tradition and hue-for-magnitude is forbidden

workflow.action: Encode taxonomy hue, kin shades and yield brightness
workflow.description: Assign distinct CVD-safe role hues (<=~7-8) with analogous kin shades, and map high-yield weight to a dark-theme-safe brightness ramp orthogonal to hue
workflow.gate: distinct role hues under the ~7-8 cap, analogous kin shades, and an orthogonal monotone yield brightness ramp are specified

workflow.action: Encode discrete mastery states and the corner intensity dot
workflow.description: Color green=known/gray=unasked aligned with the app bars and move weakness intensity to a separate corner dot token
workflow.gate: discrete green/gray states align with APP_RECON §5.9 bars and weakness intensity is on the corner dot, not the fill

workflow.description: Validate hues under CVD simulation, ban red-green-only distinctions, and require a non-color redundant channel per meaning
workflow.gate: the palette passes CVD simulation, no distinction is red-green-only, and every meaning has a grayscale-decodable second channel

workflow.action: Apply gamut and WCAG contrast gates
workflow.description: Gamut-map every color and check each pair against WCAG contrast on the dark theme, clamping the ramp's dark end to the floor
workflow.gate: every token is gamut-mapped and every pair meets the ~4.5:1/~3:1 WCAG targets after clamping

workflow.action: Build the categorical/sequential/diverging palettes and validate in situ
workflow.description: Construct the three palette families in a perceptual space for graph and charts, then validate small-mark appearance against simultaneous contrast
workflow.gate: categorical/sequential/diverging families are built per data type in a perceptual space and validated at mark size on the dark theme

workflow.action: Aggregate color honestly across semantic zoom
workflow.description: Define truthful cluster hue (dominant or neutral-mixed) and honest brightness aggregation, folding mastery dots into a weak-count badge
workflow.gate: cluster color aggregates truthfully with no false category or implied precision and dots fold into a badge at low zoom

workflow.action: Route everything through tokens and issue the verdict
workflow.description: Compute every color as a gated semantic token and commit to the go/no-go color-system verdict
workflow.gate: all color is a gated computed token and the go stack and no-gos are stated with the four-part acceptance rule

dominance_rules.rule: A perceptual space dominates sRGB/HSL for any color that encodes a scale
dominance_rules.rationale: equal steps in sRGB/HSL are perceptually unequal so a scale built there mis-encodes magnitude
dominance_rules.trigger: a sequential, diverging or brightness ramp is being authored
dominance_rules.action: build the ramp in CIELAB-HCL or OKLCH, never in HSL/sRGB

dominance_rules.rule: Lightness dominates hue for encoding an ordered quantity
dominance_rules.rationale: hue has no perceptual order so a rainbow ramp cannot be decoded in sequence
dominance_rules.trigger: a magnitude (yield, mastery, calibration) needs a color encoding
dominance_rules.action: encode magnitude in a monotone lightness ramp and reserve hue for unordered categories

dominance_rules.rationale: an extra hue that only the median viewer can distinguish excludes ~8% of users
dominance_rules.trigger: adding a taxonomy hue beyond the CVD-separable set
dominance_rules.action: cap hues at the CVD-separable count and add a shape/glyph channel instead

dominance_rules.rule: The WCAG contrast floor dominates the yield ramp's dark end
dominance_rules.rationale: an illegible dim node or label fails accessibility regardless of how well it encodes low yield
dominance_rules.trigger: the yield ramp would darken a node or label below the contrast floor
dominance_rules.action: clamp the dark end to the higher of the visibility and WCAG floors and outline failing marks

dominance_rules.rule: A separate state token dominates overloading the node fill
dominance_rules.rationale: one fill cannot honestly carry role, yield and mastery at once
dominance_rules.trigger: mastery state is about to recolor the whole node fill
dominance_rules.action: keep role+yield on the fill and put mastery/intensity on the corner dot token

dominance_rules.rule: A non-color redundant channel dominates color-only distinctions for anything critical
dominance_rules.rationale: color alone fails under CVD, grayscale and small marks
dominance_rules.trigger: a critical distinction is carried by color alone
dominance_rules.action: add a grayscale-decodable channel (shape, position, size, label) so the distinction survives without color

dominance_rules.rule: Honest aggregation dominates a confident single cluster color
dominance_rules.rationale: a crisp single hue on a mixed cluster asserts a category the detail does not support
dominance_rules.trigger: a zoomed-out cluster spans multiple roles or magnitudes
dominance_rules.action: use a dominant hue only when role-coherent, else neutral/mixed, and never put aggregate magnitude in hue

dominance_rules.rule: A gated computed token dominates a hardcoded hex
dominance_rules.rationale: a raw hex escapes the gamut, CVD and contrast gates and cannot be re-tuned centrally
dominance_rules.trigger: a component is about to set a raw color value
dominance_rules.action: reference a semantic token computed and gate-checked in the single build step

dominance_rules.rule: An ESTIMATE-to-source-verify tag dominates an asserted color-science number
dominance_rules.rationale: no WCAG ratio, JND or palette claim is source-verified in EXTERNAL_RECON here
dominance_rules.trigger: a color-science threshold is about to be stated or hardcoded
dominance_rules.action: tag it ESTIMATE-to-source-verify and confirm exact values in the L1 research pass before committing

anti_rework_rules.rule: Fix the channel-to-meaning map (hue=category, lightness=magnitude) before assigning any color
anti_rework_rules.prevents: building a hue-for-magnitude rainbow that must be torn out and re-encoded as a lightness ramp

anti_rework_rules.rule: Choose the perceptual space before building any ramp
anti_rework_rules.prevents: authoring ramps in HSL and reworking every one when perceived lightness proves non-monotone

anti_rework_rules.rule: Run CVD simulation on the hue set before finalizing taxonomy colors
anti_rework_rules.prevents: shipping a red-green role pair that collapses and having to reassign the whole palette

anti_rework_rules.rule: Reserve a separate token for mastery state before designing the node fill
anti_rework_rules.prevents: overloading the fill with three meanings and having to re-separate them into fill plus dot

anti_rework_rules.rule: Apply gamut and contrast gates as colors are defined, not after
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a finished palette that clamps out of gamut or fails contrast and must be rebuilt

anti_rework_rules.rule: Validate colors at true mark size on the dark theme before locking them
anti_rework_rules.prevents: swatch-tuned hues that merge on small nodes and force a late re-tune

anti_rework_rules.rule: Route color through computed tokens from the start
anti_rework_rules.prevents: scattered hardcoded hex that has to be hunted down and centralized later

anti_rework_rules.rule: Tag every color-science number ESTIMATE-to-source-verify when first written
anti_rework_rules.prevents: hardcoding an unverified WCAG ratio or JND that a later source check overturns app-wide

iteration_protocol.trigger: the color-science references (CIELAB, WCAG ratios, Okabe-Ito, viridis, OKLCH claims) are source-verified in an L1 research pass
iteration_protocol.action: replace each ESTIMATE-to-source-verify tag with a cited FACT and correct any threshold that differs

iteration_protocol.trigger: a graph library is chosen and its color/rendering API constrains the design
iteration_protocol.action: reconcile the token system and channel assignments with the library's capabilities

iteration_protocol.trigger: a CVD simulation or in-situ test flags a collapsed or illegible color pair
iteration_protocol.action: re-space the hues, raise small-mark chroma, or add a redundant channel and re-run the gates

iteration_protocol.trigger: the app changes its MasteryBars thresholds or dark-theme background
iteration_protocol.action: re-align the discrete mastery states and re-check the yield ramp's usable band and contrast

iteration_protocol.trigger: a CIELAB-vs-OKLCH benchmark on this app's palette settles the space choice
iteration_protocol.action: commit the primary perceptual space and regenerate the tokens in it

iteration_protocol.trigger: the semantic-zoom clustering changes how members group
iteration_protocol.action: revisit the cluster hue/brightness aggregation and the dot-to-badge folding

iteration_protocol.trigger: a new per-node meaning or chart quantity must be encoded
iteration_protocol.action: reassess the channel budget and add a palette family or redundant channel rather than overloading an existing one

priority_rationale: The problem frame and the perceptual-space choice come first because they decide the coordinate system every later color is expressed in and rule out the sRGB/HSL spaces that would mis-encode magnitude; the channel-to-meaning map is the spine that assigns hue to taxonomy category and lightness to yield/mastery magnitude, and the taxonomy-hue, kin-shade, yield-brightness, mastery-state and corner-dot nodes are its direct applications; the accessibility layer (CVD-safety, redundant encoding, gamut and WCAG contrast, palette construction and simultaneous contrast) constrains and validates those encodings so they work for all users on the dark theme; and the semantic-zoom aggregation, computed token system and final verdict come last because they compose every upstream encoding into one honest, gated, re-tunable color system with an explicit no-go on rainbow ramps, red-green-only distinctions and hardcoded hex.
